title: Microsoft's Brad Smith Defends Overseas Data Centres After Trump's Penalty Threat
excerpt: On Face the Nation, Smith split AI training sites from the cloud facilities that must sit near customers — while the Treasury secretary said he had not discussed Trump's proposal with him.
body:
• Microsoft President Brad Smith, on CBS's "Face the Nation" on Sunday, split data centres into two kinds: facilities that train the most advanced AI models, and the far larger number that deliver everyday cloud services — streaming, gaming and business software — which he said must sit close to the customers who use them.
  • President Donald Trump said at a Friday news conference that the United States would not allow data centres to move to other countries and threatened "tremendous penalties" on companies that build them abroad. No rate, mechanism, start date or list of covered countries has been announced.
  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he had not discussed the proposal's details with Trump, and read the president's concern as stopping a major transfer of technology overseas.
  • For India: Microsoft's $17.5 billion investment plan for 2026–2029, covering cloud and AI infrastructure in Chennai, Hyderabad and Pune, was not named as a target by either Smith or Bessent, and Smith announced no change to it. There is nothing for Indian customers or employees to act on yet — the proposal has no published details.

Microsoft President Brad Smith has pushed back against President Donald Trump's threat to penalise American technology companies that build data centres abroad, arguing that most data centres are not AI training sites at all but local infrastructure that has to sit near the people it serves. Speaking on CBS's "Face the Nation" on Sunday, Smith drew a line between two kinds of facility that the debate, in his telling, has been treating as one.

Two kinds of data centre

The first kind trains the most advanced artificial intelligence models. On those, Smith conceded ground: there was room to discuss keeping that training in the United States. The second kind — the majority, he said — provides cloud services: the software, storage and processing power that customers rent over a network instead of running on their own equipment. Those services increasingly carry AI features inside business applications and video games, but their defining requirement is proximity.

"They're cloud services to stream a video, play a video game, run your business. And those have to be located close to customers."

— Brad Smith, President, Microsoft

Smith used Finland to make the point concrete. A facility serving Finnish customers, he argued, cannot simply be replaced by one in the United States: "You can't support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey." Latency and local service delivery, not cost arbitrage, are what place these buildings where they are.

Smith was careful not to dismiss the president outright. "My sense is that the president is making an important point, but there's some critical nuance we need to think about as well," he said. His closing argument was that keeping advanced AI development in America and operating facilities near overseas customers are different questions requiring different policy decisions.

A threat without details — so far

Trump made the threat at a Friday news conference, saying the United States would not allow data centres to move to other countries and promising "tremendous penalties" against companies attempting to do so; other reporting of the same remarks described the penalty as a "tremendous tax." The president gave no rate, no mechanism, no start date and no indication of whether projects already announced would be covered.

The vagueness extends inside his own administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who attended the news conference, said he had not spoken to Trump about the proposal afterwards. Bessent interpreted the concern behind it as preventing a major transfer of technology overseas, and drew a comparison with semiconductor manufacturing, where he argued that dependence on production abroad had created a strategic vulnerability the administration is trying to address. He also said technology companies needed to explain their plans better to Americans and rebuild trust with the communities that host data centres.

What it means for India

The debate lands directly on one of the largest technology investments ever announced in India. In December 2025, Microsoft committed $17.5 billion over 2026–2029 to cloud and AI infrastructure, skills and ongoing operations in India, building on an earlier $3 billion commitment and including expanded data-centre regions in Chennai, Hyderabad and Pune. The IANS report notes that this is a multiyear commitment, not money already spent — which is precisely why an undefined penalty regime creates uncertainty rather than an immediate bill.

Neither Smith nor Bessent identified India as a target of the proposed restrictions, and Smith announced no change to Microsoft's international investments on Sunday. The distinction Smith is pressing — training facilities versus customer-facing cloud regions — would matter enormously to how any eventual policy treats the India build-out, since the Chennai, Hyderabad and Pune regions exist to serve customers in and around India. Until the administration publishes an actual proposal, that is where the story rests: a presidential threat, an industry argument about what a data centre is for, and a Treasury secretary who has not yet discussed the details with the president.
